937 [isolate -> prune] Gate each model's inference loop with a skip flag. To evaluate a candidate, disable all other members and submit the candidate alone to gauge its standalone quality. Iterate on its checkpoints or backbone variants in isolation. Once satisfied, re-enable all members, adjust blend weights, and verify the full ensemble improves over the previous best before adopting the 
646 [runtime -> threshold] After binning, check whether the result has more than one distinct value. If it has collapsed to a constant, fall back to the original continuous predictions for that column to preserve ranking information.
676 [diverse -> embeddings] Extract sentence embeddings from one or more pretrained encoders for each text field, compute pairwise similarity features (e.g., dot-product between question and answer embeddings), one-hot encode categorical metadata, concatenate everything into a feature matrix, train lightweight models on it, and blend their predictions with the transformer's via rank-averaging.
848 [diverse -> prune] Swap individual members one at a time, replacing each with an alternative checkpoint, and submit to evaluate. A member that is individually weaker can still improve the ensemble if it is sufficiently diverse. Keep the swap only if the overall metric improves; otherwise revert.
1201 [cache -> selection] Re-run feature selection from scratch whenever the candidate feature set changes, rather than loading a previously saved selection. Save the new result for future runs only after confirming it includes and fairly evaluates all new candidates.
1226 [isolate -> objective] Audit the custom objective's gradient and Hessian computation for correctness. Ensure the Hessian is a proper second derivative rather than a placeholder (e.g., all ones). Remove unnecessary complexity like per-class weighting that can destabilize training. Move shared constants out of the function to avoid accidental redefinition. Test each simplification incremental
1503 [isolate -> prune] Keep all other ensemble members fixed while iterating on the new component. First validate the new model in isolation or with a fixed baseline ensemble, then toggle only its inclusion to measure its marginal contribution. Avoid changing multiple members' inclusion at the same time as architectural edits.
93 [isolate -> tree_rate] Reset the uncertain parameters to library defaults in one step, keeping only the parameters whose effect is well understood (e.g., learning rate, number of rounds). Compare validation performance against the previous run. Re-introduce parameters one at a time only if the default-based run is worse, so each parameter's marginal contribution is visible.
633 [isolate -> checkpoint] After introducing the architecture and preprocessing change, immediately try multiple saved checkpoints before concluding the change is harmful. A single checkpoint may underperform due to training variance; the best checkpoint under the new setup may still beat the old best.
532 [weights_tune -> seeds] Test swapping the seed model independently from weight changes. If the swap degrades performance, revert it. The seed model's predictions anchor the blend, so a model with consistently strong per-subgroup performance is preferable as the seed, even if another model has a marginally higher overall score.

survival 503 The evaluation metric is concordance-based (ranking metric), and the raw data includes censored event times and event indicators. Standard regression models (gradient-boosted trees) will be used. Use a non-parametric survival estimator (e.g., Kaplan-Meier) to compute survival probabilities at each patient's event time, then use these probabilities as the regression target. This handles censoring naturally and produces a continuous target whose ranking aligns with the concordance metric.
group_target 405 A survival or ranking target is derived from a global statistical estimate (e.g., a cumulative hazard curve). The metric averages per-subgroup performance and penalizes variance across subgroups, so a globally computed target may under-fit minority subgroups whose event distributions differ. Compute the target transform separately within each subgroup used by the equity metric, then recombine. This ensures each subgroup's target reflects its own event distribution, improving calibration where the metric measures it. Verify with the stratified metric that both mean and variance components improve.
ordinal 1104 A regression head with post-hoc threshold tuning already achieves a strong score on an ordinal prediction task measured by a ranking-correlation metric (e.g., quadratic weighted kappa). Implement a classification head that outputs softmax probabilities over ordinal classes and takes argmax. Compare its leaderboard score against the regression + optimized-rounding baseline. If classification underperforms, retain the regression approach—threshold optimization on continuous outputs often captures inter-class boundaries better than hard argmax for ordinal metrics.
target_scale 429 A scalar parameter controls how survival times or hazards are collapsed/scaled before being used as regression targets. Small changes to this factor have produced measurable leaderboard differences. Probe the parameter in small increments (e.g., steps of ~0.1) with single-variable submissions. Track the leaderboard response to map the sensitivity curve and find the local optimum. If partial recovery is seen, continue probing in the improving direction.
last 46 The dataset has multiple time-ordered rows per entity that must be collapsed to one row for a supervised model. Complex aggregations (multiple statistics per column) increase code complexity and risk pipeline bugs before a first submission exists. Start with the simplest possible aggregation (e.g., just the mean for numeric columns and count for categorical columns) to get an end-to-end working pipeline and a baseline score. Once that succeeds, incrementally add richer statistics (std, min, max, last value, nunique) one or two at a time, verifying each addition improves the score.
aggregate 48 When multiple time-ordered rows are aggregated per entity and only a single summary statistic (e.g., mean) is used, the model lacks information about trends, extremes, and variability within each entity's history. Add at minimum the last value, min, max, median, and count of unique values as groupby aggregation functions for numeric and categorical columns. This set captures recency, range, central tendency, and diversity. Expect a large score jump (several percentage points) over a mean-only baseline; further gains from adding std or custom aggregations will be smaller.
temporal 49 A baseline with standard numeric aggregations (mean, std, min, max, last) already performs well. A date column has been excluded from aggregation because it is not natively numeric. Try simple transformations first: days-since-reference-date (global max or per-group max), then include in standard aggregations or take only the 'last' value. Submit after each variant and compare to baseline. If no variant improves the score after several attempts, accept that the date feature adds no signal in this encoding and move on rather than continuing to iterate.
interact 62 Gradient-boosted trees can learn arbitrary splits and interactions internally. The baseline already includes per-customer aggregations (mean, std, min, max, first, last) and simple derived features. Test a small representative subset of the proposed interaction features first and check the leaderboard or validation score before expanding. If the initial subset does not improve the score, the tree model is likely already capturing those interactions, and further sweeping of variants is unlikely to help. Abandon the direction early rather than iterating through many column combinations.
ngrams 1229 A text-based model uses sparse n-gram features alongside engineered features. The practitioner considers reducing the n-gram range to cut dimensionality and noise. Avoid removing the lowest-order n-grams (e.g., unigrams) from word-level features, as they often carry the most discriminative signal. If a score drop follows tightening, restore the original range before attributing the loss to other simultaneous changes. Change n-gram ranges independently from other feature modifications to isolate their effect.
embeddings 1260 Ad-hoc extraction code keeps being added and removed because it is fragile, slow, or hard to maintain. The embeddings need to feed into a downstream gradient-boosted ensemble. Factor extraction into a reusable pipeline: a dataset wrapper, a pooling function (e.g., mean-pool over token hidden states), and a top-level function that loads the model once, iterates in batches on GPU, normalizes the output vectors (e.g., L2), and returns dense arrays. Keep this separate from the training loop so it can be swapped or precomputed independently.
linguistic 686 A fine-tuned pretrained language model is the primary model, but the targets include aspects (e.g., thoroughness, formatting quality) that may correlate with simple surface features like text length or sentence count, which the model may not leverage well on its own. Compute surface-level text features (word counts, sentence counts, categorical indicators), standardize them, and concatenate them with the language model's pooled output before the prediction head. Retrain with these additional inputs and verify improvement on the leaderboard or validation metric.
topics 1193 A topic model with automatic topic count selection and remotely-loaded embedding models are used to create features for a gradient-boosted model. The pipeline runs but has not yet been submitted. Fix the number of topics to a small explicit value rather than using automatic selection, so features are stable across train and test. Use locally cached embedding checkpoints to avoid download failures and ensure reproducibility. Adjust clustering granularity to roughly match the number of target classes.
text_format 178 A single model checkpoint is underperforming a previously established ensemble baseline, and the practitioner is searching for easy gains without retraining. Test changing the random seed and increasing the maximum token length at inference. Expect minimal impact: seed affects only stochastic elements (e.g., dropout if left on), and longer tokens help only if inputs were being truncated. If the gap to the ensemble persists, return to ensembling rather than continuing single-model tweaks.
retrieval 245 A strong stacked ensemble of fine-tuned language models already achieves a competitive score on a small text regression task. The practitioner considers adding a new feature source based on semantic similarity retrieval from training data. Implement a retrieval feature generator that encodes texts with a pretrained bi-encoder, finds top-k nearest training examples, and uses their labels as features for the meta-learner. Compare the new ensemble score against the baseline. If the retrieval-augmented version scores worse, keep the original ensemble and only blend in the new features at a small weight, or discard them entirely.
spectrum 803 An inference pipeline using spectrogram-based features has reached a plateau. The spectral transform parameters (e.g., FFT window length) have not yet been tuned at inference time. Try adjusting the FFT window length (which controls frequency vs. time resolution trade-off) at inference to match what was used during training. If the parameter was not used during training, changing it at inference will create a train-test mismatch and hurt performance. Verify by submitting and comparing; revert if the score degrades.
crop 757 A pipeline uses features from multiple overlapping or adjacent time windows around the labeled segment. It is unclear whether the flanking windows add signal or just add noise and compute cost. Ablate by removing the flanking windows, submit or validate with center-only, then restore them and compare. If the flanking windows yield even a small consistent gain, keep them; the cost is justified because ensembles amplify small per-component improvements.
filter_signal 954 Reducing the sampling rate and narrowing the bandpass filter saves computation but may discard informative high-frequency content. A prior best result used the higher rate and wider band. Test the lower sampling rate and narrower filter as a pair against the original settings. If the score degrades, revert both. Physiological signals (especially brain activity) can carry discriminative information in higher frequency bands, so do not aggressively downsample or narrow the filter without empirical validation.
normalize_signal 945 A pretrained backbone trained on natural RGB images is being fed non-RGB input (e.g., grayscale or multi-channel spectrograms). The hypothesis is that colormap-based RGB conversion better matches the pretrained feature detectors. Apply a standard colormap (e.g., jet) to map scalar spectrogram values to 3-channel RGB, then feed to the pretrained backbone. Compare against the baseline input format on the leaderboard or validation. Be aware this may not help and can even hurt if the original channel encoding already carries useful information.
reshape 940 A pipeline combining spectrograms and raw time-series signals has reached a strong baseline. The time-series branch uses fewer derived channels than available and has a suspected indexing bug in how signal windows are extracted. Fix the window extraction to use the correct sampling rate, increase the number of derived input channels, and add per-sample normalization. After making these changes, retrain or load updated checkpoints and compare the leaderboard score. If the score does not improve, the additional channels or normalization may be adding noise or the checkpoint was not properly retrained on the new inputs.
modality 792 A model has been trained with an optional auxiliary signal channel. The channel is plausibly informative but may also add noise if the model wasn't strongly trained on it or if the test distribution differs. Run inference once with the auxiliary channel enabled and once without, comparing leaderboard or validation scores. If disabling it matches or improves the score, drop it to reduce complexity and potential noise. Even a tiny improvement justifies removal because it also simplifies the pipeline.
selection 19 A tree-based model is trained on a large engineered feature set. A two-stage workflow is introduced: train once to measure feature importance, then retrain on only the top features. Validation scores (not public leaderboard) guide the choice. Start with a moderate retention ratio (e.g., one quarter), then try an aggressive cut (e.g., one tenth). If validation drops, walk the ratio back up in small increments (roughly 5–10 percentage points per trial) until the validation metric plateaus or declines. Use median importance across CV folds to rank features for stability. Expect the optimum somewhere between one quarter and one half of the original feature count for heavily engineered tabular sets.
ablate_features 31 A gradient-boosted tree model is already performing well with a large engineered feature set, and the practitioner suspects some feature groups may add noise. Test feature group removal in isolation and submit. If the score regresses, immediately revert. Do not combine feature removal with other hyperparameter changes (e.g., learning rate) in the same submission, as confounding makes it impossible to attribute the effect.
missing_drop 116 After iterative feature importance-based pruning has been done, columns with extreme missingness may still remain and can add noise or slow training without contributing signal. Identify columns with high missing-value rates and explicitly drop them before aggregation and training. Verify on validation that dropping them does not hurt the metric. This complements importance-based selection by targeting a different failure mode (sparse signal).
native 50 Gradient-boosted tree implementations can route missing values natively at each split. Mean-imputing aggregation-induced NaNs may destroy the informative signal that a group had too few observations to compute the statistic. Start by leaving NaNs for the tree model to handle natively. Only add explicit imputation if validation shows it helps. Aggregation-induced NaNs (e.g., std with one row) often carry information (small group size), so preserving them as missing is a reasonable default.
impute 527 Some model families (e.g., gradient-boosted trees) handle missing values natively, while others (e.g., random forests, linear models, neural nets) require explicit imputation. A shared feature pipeline that uses one strategy may silently degrade models that need a different treatment. Make the feature-generation function model-aware by accepting a model identifier and branching on it: apply the imputation strategy each model family expects (e.g., sentinel value for tree models that lack native NaN support, median/mean for others). This ensures every ensemble member receives correctly preprocessed inputs.
round_features 52 Gradient-boosted trees already discretize features at split points, but explicit rounding can reduce noise and effectively bin near-identical values, sometimes improving generalization slightly. Round continuous features to a small number of decimal places, replace the originals, and evaluate on the leaderboard or validation set. Expect only a marginal gain; treat it as a low-effort addition rather than a major lever.
tree_family 458 A linear or semi-parametric survival model is the current baseline, and pre-trained tree-based models are available. The metric values both discrimination and fairness across subgroups. Replace the survival model inference with gradient-boosted tree predictions, rank-averaging across fold models. Critically, remove all preprocessing code specific to the old model rather than layering the new model on top; leftover incompatible preprocessing can silently corrupt predictions and cause a large score drop.
classical 456 Two libraries offer similar linear survival models (proportional hazards / penalized Cox). The current model already scores competitively, and the candidate is conceptually similar rather than a fundamentally different model family. Swap the model backend and compare on the leaderboard. Expect minimal change when the underlying model class is nearly identical; reserve effort for trying a genuinely different model family (e.g., gradient-boosted trees) if the swap shows no gain.
native_api 2 A high-level API is already producing predictions blended at very small weight into a strong baseline submission. The practitioner wants finer control (early stopping, iteration selection). Switch to the native training API with a held-out validation set and early stopping. Compare the leaderboard score at the same blend weight. If the score does not improve, the gain from API-level control is negligible and effort is better spent elsewhere (e.g., features or hyperparameters).
wrapper_api 159 The native low-level training API requires manual dataset wrapper objects and raw score conversion; the library also offers a scikit-learn-compatible estimator API. Use the scikit-learn-compatible estimator class. It handles dataset wrapping internally, provides a predict_proba method for direct probability output, and accepts early-stopping callbacks in the fit call, reducing boilerplate and integration friction.
distribution 1122 A regression model outputs continuous predictions that must be discretized into ordinal labels. The evaluation metric is quadratic weighted kappa, which is sensitive to both per-sample accuracy and marginal distribution alignment. The target distribution is approximately known from training data. Sort all test predictions by their continuous value and assign discrete labels so cumulative counts match the expected distribution. Compare the resulting metric against per-sample optimized-threshold rounding. Be aware that distribution matching ignores per-sample confidence and can hurt metrics that reward correct individual assignments; if it underperforms threshold rounding, revert.
ties 652 A rank-correlation metric (e.g., Spearman) assigns averaged ranks to tied values, which can reduce correlation with the true ranking. After normalization or rounding, many predictions may share the same float value. Add negligible random noise (e.g., Gaussian with standard deviation many orders of magnitude smaller than the prediction range) to break ties before submission. This preserves the intended ordering while ensuring the rank-based metric sees distinct values.

136 Once EDA insights are captured, aggressively remove or comment out plotting and verbose inspection cells, suppress non-critical warnings, and replace ad-hoc transformations with reusable preprocessing objects. This keeps the notebook fast and focused for the modeling phase that follows.
141 After confirming correctness, clean up in order: first disable periodic training metric logging, then remove system diagnostic commands, then remove debug print statements from data processing. This layered approach avoids losing diagnostic information before bugs are resolved.
419 Refactor the notebook into an inference-only pipeline: remove all training and model-definition code, call external prediction scripts via shell commands, load their outputs, apply the fixed blend coefficients and any post-processing, and write the final submission. Separate the structural refactor (replacing code with script calls and placeholder coefficients) from filling in the exact numeric constants, so each step can be verified independently.
461 Always write the final predictions to the exact filename the platform expects (typically 'submission.csv'). When refactoring inference code, verify the output filename has not been inadvertently changed.
640 After discretization, check each column for degeneracy (all values identical). For any degenerate column, revert to the original continuous predictions. Prefer an exact constant-check over a variance threshold, as the threshold can be fragile. Also rescale surviving discretized columns to a standard range to keep scales consistent.
646 After binning, check whether the result has more than one distinct value. If it has collapsed to a constant, fall back to the original continuous predictions for that column to preserve ranking information.
647 Inspect an environment-dependent artifact at startup (e.g., the size of a provided output template, the existence of certain directories, or an environment variable) and set the debug flag programmatically based on a simple threshold or check.
654 Verify that model weights are actually loaded and predictions contain real signal by checking a few outputs manually. If in-notebook training is infeasible (time/memory), switch to loading precomputed predictions from external scripts or pre-uploaded artifacts. Add try/except fallback to known-good prediction files so the ensemble always contains valid predictions rather than garbage.
655 For each model in the ensemble, wrap the file-loading step in a try/except. On failure, fall back to a pre-uploaded set of known-good predictions stored as a separate data asset. After merging all available predictions, fill any remaining NaNs and re-normalize before writing the submission. This guarantees the submission always contains meaningful predictions even when some models fail.
659 Start with a manually chosen subset of columns where the transformation is most justified (e.g., columns with clearly discrete structure). Avoid applying it globally. Then incrementally add columns one at a time, submitting after each addition, and keep only those that improve the metric. Stop when additions no longer help.
679 Use the fixed holdout only for local debugging and hyperparameter selection. For the final submission, disable the holdout and train on all available data using k-fold cross-validation, so every example contributes to the model. Compare leaderboard scores with and without the holdout to confirm the effect.
697 Before iterating on postprocessing or swapping checkpoints, verify that the model produces non-degenerate, varying outputs across test samples (e.g., print summary statistics, check variance per target). A constant or near-constant prediction vector will yield the same rank correlation no matter how it is rescaled. Diagnose the forward pass (tokenizer alignment, weight loading, input construction) first.
710 Avoid adding random noise to predictions when the evaluation metric is rank-based, as it can only degrade signal. Clipping to avoid exact 0/1 is also unnecessary for rank metrics. Use raw model outputs or deterministic post-processing (e.g., quantile mapping) instead.
852 Comment out the install step and re-run inference multiple times. Compare the resulting score distribution against the known run-to-run variance from before the change. If scores stay within the established noise band, the dependency is confirmed unused and can be permanently removed.
923 First, delete all dead code for the removed model family to reduce complexity and runtime. Then systematically try different epoch checkpoints for each fold of the remaining models, submitting to see if a different combination yields a small score improvement. Expect only marginal gains (on the order of noise) from checkpoint swapping alone.
933 Re-enable all optimized components and submit the full weighted blend. Expect the blend to outperform every individual component and potentially beat the prior best, since each member is now individually stronger. If the blend does not improve, a component may be hurting diversity and should be removed.
961 Remove the underperforming branch and instead invest the computational budget in improving the quality of existing inputs (higher resolution, better filtering, correct time-window alignment).                     supported.add(child_id)
    assert supported == children, ('"'Option lacks a positive selection check', node['id'], children - supported)
print(f'Items placed: {len(placed)}')
print(f'Unassigned: {len(unassigned)}')
